subject: chemistry

moments.title: Werner's coordination theory
moments.body: Werner explains why CoCl3·6NH3 behaves differently from Cr(NH3)6Cl3: octahedral coordination spheres around the metal centre. He wins the 1913 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Transition-metal complexes have defined geometries — usually octahedral.

moments.title: Crystal field theory
moments.who: Hans Bethe, then John Van Vleck
moments.body: Bethe and Van Vleck explain transition-metal colours and magnetism via crystal-field splitting of d-orbitals. The colour of copper sulphate gets a quantum-mechanical explanation.
moments.takeaway: Why is copper sulphate blue? Quantum mechanics answers.

moments.title: Ferrocene
moments.body: Ferrocene — an iron atom sandwiched between two cyclopentadienyl rings — is synthesised. Its structure defies classical bonding rules. Wilkinson and Fischer share the 1973 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Organometallic chemistry is born. The boundary between organic and inorganic blurs.

moments.title: Wilkinson's catalyst
moments.body: Wilkinson's RhCl(PPh3)3 catalyses hydrogenation under mild conditions. Homogeneous catalysis becomes a major industrial method.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Transition-metal catalysis (Suzuki, Heck, Negishi 2010 Nobel; metathesis 2005 Nobel) underpins modern drug synthesis. Cisplatin saves thousands of cancer patients annually.
now.open_questions: Can earth-abundant metals (Fe, Co, Ni) replace precious ones (Pt, Pd, Rh, Ir) in catalysis?

reflection: Werner married a Catholic and refused to be baptised Lutheran for an academic post — a 19th-century stand for principle. How does professional pressure shape scientific identity?
